With the parish priest of Santo Spirito
Early July. Matei and Giulia, with Viola in her pram, are talking to Don Lorenzo, the parish priest of Santo Spirito, about the christening.
Right, you two, let's talk about the christening. Who are the godparents?
The godmother is Ilinca, Matei's sister, who arrives from Sibiu on Thursday. She's a doctor.
And the godfather is Gennaro, Giulia's brother, whom we've asked not to bring any fireworks.
(laughs) A wise decision. And the christening gown?
It's the one in which my grandmother Assunta was christened, in 1934. My great-grandmother made it — we still have her sewing machine in Sorrento.
How lovely. Did you know this is the church where Graziella and Aldo got married?
Yes, that's exactly why we chose it. Without them we wouldn't be here.
And the date?
The twelfth of July, the day Pietro turns ten. He's the boy without whom we'd never have found the name.
Very good. Is there anything else you'd like to talk to me about?
Yes… My father, Ion, would like to bring a bottle of pălincă, whose strength I'd rather not tell you.
(laughs) First I'll bless it. Then, just to be sure, I'll taste it.

1. Il quale, la quale, i quali, le quali
"Il quale" also means "who / which", like "che", but it AGREES in gender and number. You use it in formal style or when "che" would be ambiguous:
il quale
Ho visto il fratello di Giulia, il quale arriva domani.
I saw Giulia's brother, who arrives tomorrow.
la quale
La madrina è Ilinca, la quale è medico.
The godmother is Ilinca, who is a doctor.
i quali
I nonni, i quali vivono a Sibiu, arriveranno in treno.
The grandparents, who live in Sibiu, will arrive by train.
le quali
Le zie, le quali abitano a Napoli, porteranno i dolci.
The aunts, who live in Naples, will bring the sweets.
"Il fratello di Giulia, che arriva domani" — who is arriving, the brother or Giulia? With "il quale" it's clear: the brother. With "la quale": Giulia.
2. Preposition + il quale
After a preposition you can't use "che". You use "il quale", and the preposition merges with the article:
di → del quale
Il libro del quale ti ho parlato.
The book I told you about.
a → al quale
Gennaro, al quale abbiamo chiesto…
Gennaro, whom we asked…
in → nella quale
La chiesa nella quale si sono sposati.
The church in which they got married.
con → con la quale
La veste con la quale è stata battezzata.
The gown in which she was christened.
senza → senza il quale
Il bambino senza il quale…
The boy without whom…
NOT "la chiesa che si sono sposati" and NOT "la chiesa dove che". After a preposition: "nella quale" or "in cui".
3. Cui after prepositions
"Cui" is the shorter, more common option in speech. It never changes (no gender or number):
With "cui"
With "il quale"
la persona a cui ho scritto
la persona alla quale ho scritto
the person I wrote to
il libro di cui ti ho parlato
il libro del quale ti ho parlato
the book I told you about
la chiesa in cui si sono sposati
la chiesa nella quale si sono sposati
the church where they got married
gli amici con cui esco
gli amici con i quali esco
the friends I go out with
With "a" the preposition can be dropped: "la persona cui ho scritto" (written, elegant style).
4. Il cui, la cui, i cui, le cui (whose)
"Il cui" expresses possession. The article agrees with the thing POSSESSED, not with the owner. "Cui" stays the same:
My great-grandmother, whose sewing machine we still have…
The professor, whose books I always read…
Ernesto, whose diary is on the table…

English "whose" never changes, but in Italian you must choose the article: "la cui macchina" — "la" agrees with the thing owned (macchina, feminine), while "cui" doesn't change. "Il professore, LA cui figlia…" (figlia, feminine), even though the professor is masculine.
5. In cui, per cui: time, place, reason
il giorno in cui
Il giorno in cui Pietro compie dieci anni.
The day Pietro turns ten.
il motivo per cui
È il motivo per cui l’abbiamo scelta.
la città in cui / dove
La città in cui (dove) sono nato.
The town where I was born.
per cui (= quindi)
Era tardi, per cui siamo andati via.
It was late, so we left.
In speech, "per cui" at the start of a clause often means "so": "Non avevo soldi, per cui sono rimasto a casa."

Il battesimo di Viola

On the twelfth of July, the day Pietro turned ten, the church of Santo Spirito was as full as at Christmas. There were the Neapolitans, who had come in a whole coach, the Romanians, who had come on four trains with three connections, and the Florentines, who had come on foot, but half an hour late, as always.

Viola was wearing the christening gown in which Grandma Assunta had been christened, in 1934, in Sorrento. It was a white linen gown, twice as long as the baby, with fine lace whose story Assunta told to anyone willing to listen: her mother had made it by hand, in three months, during the winter when Vesuvius had made the windows shake.

Ilinca had arrived from Sibiu on Thursday with Radu, the boyfriend the whole family had grown fond of by now. She was terribly nervous. She had spent two nights learning by heart the responses of the rite in Italian, which Matei had written down for her. Gennaro, on the other hand, hadn't learned a thing. "I'm Neapolitan," he had said. "I've known christenings since birth."

Pietro had the most important job, which he was very proud of: carrying the lit candle up to the altar. He was wearing a new white shirt and the watch with the blue strap Matei had given him two years before. He walked slowly, very seriously, his eyes fixed on the flame, as if he were carrying the Olympic torch.

Professor Bellini was sitting in the third row, next to Signor Franco, with whom he had made friends at the wedding. In his pocket he had the old black-and-white photograph of his grandfather Ernesto, which usually never left the drawer of his desk. That day, though, he had decided to bring it with him. "That way he can see too," he had told Franco, who had nodded without asking any questions, as real friends do.

Don Lorenzo, an elderly priest with a deep voice, began the ceremony. When he asked the godparents whether they were ready to help the parents, Ilinca answered "Sì, lo sono" with such a sweet Romanian accent that half the church smiled. Gennaro answered "Sissignore!", like a soldier, and the other half of the church burst out laughing.

Then came the moment of the water. Everyone expected Viola to cry: all babies cry when the cold water touches their head. But not Viola. She looked at Don Lorenzo with her big dark eyes, opened her mouth, and laughed. A small, clear laugh, the first of her life, which rang out beneath Brunelleschi's columns.

Don Lorenzo stopped, surprised. "In forty years of christenings," he said into the microphone, "this is the first time a baby has laughed. I think this little girl has already understood something we grown-ups always forget." Graziella, sitting in the front row next to the empty seat where Aldo would have sat, dried her eyes with the handkerchief in which she had kept Ernesto's brush.

After the ceremony there was a party in the garden behind the trattoria, under the wisteria Aldo had planted in 1980. Doina and Rosaria had been cooking together for two days, in a language neither country would have recognised but which worked perfectly. Ion had brought the famous bottle of pălincă, which had been blessed by Don Lorenzo and then, to be on the safe side, tasted several times.

Towards evening Pietro blew out ten candles and made a wish, which he wouldn't talk about with anyone. Then, while everyone was eating the cake, Radu stood up. He was as pale as on the day he had met Ion. He tapped a teaspoon against his glass. "Excuse me," he said, in an Italian learned in six months of evening classes. "I'd like to say something to a person without whom my life would have no meaning."

He turned to Ilinca, who was staring at him open-mouthed. He knelt down on the grass, among the glasses and the children, and took out a small red box. "Ilinca, the woman with whom I want to spend my whole life, whose laugh is more beautiful than Viola's… will you marry me?" Ilinca looked at the ring, then at Radu, then at her father.

Ion stood up slowly. The garden was silent. He picked up the bottle of pălincă, in which only a finger was left, poured two small glasses and gave one to Radu. "Noroc," he said. Then, in Italian, looking at Gennaro: "The next wedding… in Sibiu! I told you so!" And Ilinca, laughing and crying, said yes in three languages.

That night, when everyone had gone, Matei and Giulia stayed in the garden with Viola asleep in her pram. Above them was Aldo's wisteria; in front of them, the door of the trattoria Lucia and Renzo had opened in 1950. "Do you know what?" said Giulia. "This is the house where I want Viola to grow up." Matei took her hand. There was no need to answer.
